title: Induction vs onboarding: what is the difference in regulated organizations?
description: Induction is the defined training a new starter must receive at or before starting; onboarding is the longer path to full performance. How they differ.
shortAnswer: Induction is the defined, usually mandatory, set of information and training a person must receive when they join a workplace or start a new role, often before they begin work. Onboarding is the broader process, often lasting months, that takes a new starter from first contact to full, independent performance. In regulated organizations, induction is where many legal training duties are triggered, while onboarding is where role competence is built, assessed and signed off.
keyTakeaways: Induction is a bounded event or short program with fixed content; onboarding is an extended process that includes induction.
Many laws attach training duties to the start of work, using terms such as induction, engagement, hiring, recruitment or initial assignment.
Induction proves a person was told what they must know; onboarding should prove they can do the job without supervision.
Contractors, transfers and promotions often trigger induction duties again, even when full onboarding is not repeated.
Keep induction records and competence sign offs separate but linked, so an auditor can see both what was delivered and what was verified.

sections.heading: What is the difference between induction and onboarding?

blocks.text: Induction is the specific content a person must receive on joining or changing roles; onboarding is the whole journey to productivity, of which induction is one part. The distinction matters in regulated settings because induction content is often prescribed by law or a standard, while onboarding is designed by the organization.

Usage varies by country. Australian and British workplaces tend to say induction for the mandatory safety and policy briefing; US organizations more often say onboarding for the whole process and new hire orientation for the first sessions. The concepts are the same, so define the terms in the [training policy](/guides/how-to-write-a-training-policy) and use them consistently.

sections.heading: How do induction and onboarding compare side by side?

blocks.text: They differ in duration, ownership, content and the evidence they produce. The table is a category level comparison; individual programs vary.

sections.heading: Where do laws require training at the start of work?

blocks.text: Many regulatory regimes set training duties at the moment a person starts work or changes role. These duties belong in induction, and the wording differs by regime.

blocks.text: Two consequences follow. Induction must be tracked per person with dates, because the trigger is a date. And transfers and job changes can restart a duty even for long serving staff, which is why [role based training](/glossary/role-based-training) mapped in a [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix) is the usual control.

sections.heading: Which do you need, and how should they fit together?

blocks.text: Regulated organizations need both: a tightly controlled induction that meets every start of work duty, and an onboarding process that builds and verifies competence before a person works unsupervised.

items: List every legal or standard requirement triggered by starting work, engagement, transfer or new equipment, and assign each to induction.
Deliver induction before the person is exposed to the relevant risk, and check understanding rather than relying on acknowledgment alone.
Define the role's competence requirements and the assessment for each, as part of onboarding.
Set a clear authorization point: the person works under supervision until competence is verified and signed off.
Repeat the relevant induction elements for contractors, transfers and promotions, even when the full onboarding program is not repeated.
Link induction records and competence sign offs in one person level record.

blocks.text: The full method is in [how to structure onboarding for regulated roles](/guides/how-to-structure-onboarding-for-regulated-roles), and the assessment side is covered by [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each start of work obligation as a requirement with its trigger, audience and source, separately from role competencies and their assessment points. Induction and onboarding can then be generated from the same framework, and records show both what was delivered and when each person was cleared to work alone.

faqs.q: Is induction the same as orientation?
faqs.a: Largely. Orientation is the more common US term for the first sessions a new hire attends. Whatever the label, the regulated content that must be delivered at the start of work should be defined, tracked per person and checked for understanding.

faqs.q: Do contractors need induction if they are not onboarded?
faqs.a: Often yes. Several regimes extend start of work duties to non employees, such as the PSPF requirement covering contractors at engagement and the EU Framework Directive's requirement that workers from outside undertakings receive appropriate instructions. Contractors usually receive induction without the full onboarding program.

faqs.q: How long should onboarding last in a regulated role?
faqs.a: Until the person is verified as competent for each task they will perform without supervision. That may be days for a low risk role or months for safety critical or licensed work. Set the end point by competence sign off, not by a fixed number of weeks.

faqs.q: Does a signed induction checklist prove compliance?
faqs.a: It proves delivery, not understanding. Safe Work Australia's model Code of Practice on managing risks says it is insufficient to give a worker a procedure and ask them to acknowledge it. Add a short assessment or observed check for the content that matters most.
